procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of externment under section 57 of the Bombay Police Act, directing the petitioner to remove himself outside the limits of Greater Bombay for a period of two years.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The petitioner moved the High Court of Bombay under article 226 of the Constitution against a previous order of detention under the Preventive Detention Act, 1950. He was released from detention before the petition was heard.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The petitioner filed a petition under Article 32 of the Constitution of India in the Supreme Court for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights, challenging the externment order. The Supreme Court dismissed the petition.

decision.appeal_result: In accordance with the Judgment of the majority this Petition is dismissed.

issue.issue_text: Whether an order is illegal if it is based on previous orders of discharge or acquittal of the accused.

facts: The petitioner challenged the legality of an order, arguing that it was invalid because it was based on previous instances where the petitioner had been discharged or acquitted.
law: The relevant law provides for the "subjective satisfaction" of the authorities or officers entrusted with enforcing the special provisions of the Act.
The standard for issuing such an order is not the same as the standard of evidence required for a criminal conviction in court.
application: The Court reasoned that a prior discharge or acquittal does not automatically mean the underlying accusations were baseless. Such outcomes could be due to insufficient evidence, which might have been caused by witnesses being unavailable, intimidated, or their testimony being tampered with.

The Court stated that these are matters for the subjective satisfaction of the designated officer, and it is not the Court's role to objectively re-examine the materials to determine if the order was correct.
The Court explicitly rejected the idea of a general rule that would prohibit authorities from considering previous orders of discharge or acquittal when making their decision.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that it cannot be laid down as a general proposition of law that a previous order of discharge or acquittal cannot be taken into account by authorities when issuing an order based on their subjective satisfaction.

issue.issue_text: Whether the exercise of power is not rationally related to the criterion of 'reasonableness in the interest of the public' if it is not limited by the consideration of non-availability of witnesses.

facts: The case involved a constitutional challenge to Section 57 of the Bombay Police Act, 1951, which allows for the externment of individuals.
An argument was presented that the power granted by this section was an unreasonable restriction on fundamental rights.
This argument was based on a comparison with a different provision, Section 56, which had been previously deemed reasonable.
law: Restrictions on fundamental rights, such as the freedom of movement under Article 19 of the Constitution, must be 'reasonable' and 'in the interests of the general public'.
application: A dissenting judge, Justice Jagannadhadas, argued that the power under Section 57 was unreasonable because, unlike Section 56, it did not require a finding that witnesses were unwilling to testify in public due to fear.
The judge reasoned that the reasonableness of the power in Section 56 was based on this very limitation—that it was meant for exceptional cases where evidence was difficult to obtain publicly.

He contended that since Section 57 could be invoked without considering the non-availability of witnesses, the power was not rationally related to the criterion of 'reasonableness in the interest of the public'.
reasoning.conclusion: The majority of the Supreme Court rejected this argument. By doing so, the Court held that the absence of a requirement to find that witnesses are unavailable does not make the power under Section 57 unconstitutional. The Court implicitly decided that the provisions of Section 57 and Section 56 are distinct and that the conditions laid out in Section 57 are, on their own, sufficient to constitute a reasonable restriction in the public interest.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an order is illegal if it is based on previous orders of discharge or acquittal of the accused.
appellant_arguments: The externment order is illegal because it is based on previous orders of discharge or acquittal.
Those previous orders were passed because there was not sufficient evidence to prove the charge, and therefore they should not be used as a basis for a new restrictive order.
respondent_arguments: Previous orders of discharge or acquittal can be taken into account for a preventive order.
The insufficiency of evidence in past cases may have been due to witnesses being unavailable, overawed, or tampered with, which is a valid consideration for the authorities.
The law provides for the subjective satisfaction of the authorities, not an objective re-examination of evidence by the court, to address such situations.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the exercise of power is not rationally related to the criterion of 'reasonableness in the interest of the public' if it is not limited by the consideration of non-availability of witnesses.
appellant_arguments: The procedural safeguards, such as the right of appeal and judicial review, are illusory.

The requirement to only disclose the 'general nature of the material allegations' (under section 59) makes it very difficult for the accused to defend themselves or to challenge the order in court on the grounds provided, such as the non-availability of witnesses.
respondent_arguments: The law provides sufficient safeguards against arbitrary or unfounded orders, including review by high-ranking officers, a right of appeal to the State Government, and the ability to challenge the order in court on specific procedural grounds.
One of the specific grounds for a court challenge is that the authority was not of the opinion that witnesses were unwilling to come forward, directly linking the power to this consideration.
These provisions are intended for special cases that cannot be dealt with under normal criminal procedure, justifying the different standard.

cases.case_name: Gurbachan Singh v. The State of Bombay
cases.principle: The determination of whether restrictions imposed by a law on fundamental rights are reasonable depends on both the procedural and substantive parts of that law.

cases.case_name: N. B. Khare v. State of Delhi
cases.principle: A law imposing restrictions on fundamental rights is not necessarily unconstitutional simply because it lacks a provision for an Advisory Board whose opinion is binding.

cases.case_name: State of Madras v. V. G. Row
cases.principle: The existence of an Advisory Board is not a definitive test for the constitutionality of a law; a law can be held unconstitutional for imposing unreasonable restrictions even if it provides for an Advisory Board.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: It cannot be laid down as a general proposition of law that a previous order of discharge or acquittal cannot be taken into account by authorities when making a subjective satisfaction determination for preventive measures.
obiter: The insufficiency of evidence in a prior case may have been due to witnesses not being available to depose in open court or their testimony being tampered with.
It is not for the Court to examine afresh the materials and to be satisfied that an order is correct when the legislature has provided for the subjective satisfaction of the authorities.

It cannot be laid down as a universal rule that unless there is a provision for an Advisory Board which could scrutinize the material on which the officers or authority had taken action against a person, such a legislation would be unconstitutional.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court found that the externment order was legal and the underlying law, Section 57 of the Bombay Police Act, imposes reasonable restrictions on fundamental rights. The Court reasoned that preventive measures are necessary for public safety and that an individual's right to free movement must sometimes yield to the larger interest of the community. It held that authorities can consider previous acquittals or discharges, as the insufficiency of evidence in those cases may have been due to witness intimidation, a matter left to the subjective satisfaction of the authorities and not for objective re-examination by the court. The law's reasonableness is supported by the essential requirement, established in precedent, that the power is exercised when witnesses are unwilling to testify out of fear.
legal_tests_applied: The test of 'reasonable restrictions', which requires striking a proper balance between the fundamental right of the citizen and the social control by the State in the interest of the general public.
The principle that an individual's right to reside and move freely has to yield to the larger interest of the community when necessary to maintain peace and order.
why_appellant_lost: The argument that an order is illegal if based on previous acquittals was rejected because the court cannot objectively re-examine the reasons for those acquittals; the legislature has provided for the subjective satisfaction of the authorities, who may consider that the insufficiency of evidence was due to witnesses being overawed or tampered with.

The court explicitly stated it cannot be laid down as a general proposition of law that a previous order of discharge or acquittal cannot be taken into account by authorities in such preventive proceedings.

The argument that the power is unreasonable because it is not limited by the non-availability of witnesses was rejected based on the precedent in Gurbachan Singh v. The State of Bombay, which established that it is essential for the exercise of the power that the officer believes witnesses are unwilling to come forward due to fear for their safety.
why_respondent_won: The court accepted that the insufficiency of evidence in past cases may have been due to witnesses not being available or being overawed, and that these are matters for the subjective satisfaction of the authorities, not for objective review by the court.

The court affirmed that the law's reasonableness is based on the established principle that the power is exercised when witnesses are not willing to give evidence in public due to apprehension about the safety of their person or property.

The court endorsed the underlying principle of the Act that it is desirable in the larger interests of society to restrain the freedom of a few individuals with criminal propensities so that the majority of the community can live in peace and harmony.
policy_considerations: The law is based on the principle that it is desirable in the larger interests of society that the freedom of movement and residence of a comparatively fewer number of people should be restrained so that the majority of the community may move and live in peace and harmony.
The State has a duty not only to punish offenders but also to take preventive action, based on the principle that 'Prevention is better than cure'.
The section is plainly meant to prevent a person who has been proved to be a criminal from acting in a way which may be a repetition of his criminal propensities.
